lead: Hartford is a city of renters and old multi-family homes, built along the Connecticut River. Old sewers, aging pipes and storm runoff drive most of its water damage.
risk: sewer backups, old plumbing and storm runoff
risk_short: sewer backups, old pipes, storm runoff
why: Only about one in four Hartford homes is owner-occupied, one of the lowest rates in the country. Most people live in apartments, triple-deckers and old brick buildings. About 40% of homes were built before 1940, with cast-iron drains, old supply lines and steam heat. When a pipe fails in a multi-unit building, water can reach several units before anyone finds the source.

Hartford has a long history with water. After floods in 1936 and 1938, the city built dikes along the Connecticut River and buried the Park River in a concrete conduit under the city. Many older neighborhoods still have combined sewers that carry rain and sewage together. In a heavy storm, those pipes fill and back up into basements through floor drains.
image_alt: Black-and-white photo of workers plastering walls
image_caption: Older Hartford buildings often need walls opened and replastered after a backup.
problems: Older homes in Frog Hollow, Parkville
Pre-1940 homes in Asylum Hill, West End
tips: Install a backwater valve on the basement floor drain.
Add sewer backup coverage to your policy; it is usually extra.
Landlords: check radiators and steam pipes before each winter.
Tenants: report leaks in writing and take photos right away.
areas: Calls come from the West End, Asylum Hill, Frog Hollow, the South End, Blue Hills, Parkville, Clay Arsenal and Barry Square, plus West Hartford, East Hartford and Wethersfield.

faq.q: Why does sewage come up into my Hartford basement in storms?
faq.a: Many Hartford neighborhoods have combined sewers. In heavy rain, they fill up, and water backs up through the lowest drain in a building. A backwater valve can stop most of it. Sewage cleanup needs disinfection, so call a pro rather than mopping it up.
